title: Mujina into the Deep
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: In a near-future Japan where rights are tied to a card that can be lost or bought, people without one are mujina with no legal protection. Ubume, a thirty-year-old mujina assassin, goes on the run after a failed job and, with overworked game developer Terumi, takes in Juno, a fifteen-year-old who lost her card to the people exploiting her; Ubume agrees to work off the huge price of Juno's new rights.
life_message: In a society that sells human rights, people without protection survive by forming their own fragile bonds.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Without legal protection, mujina settle matters by their own blades.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Surveillance state is the threat; outlaws live outside its rules.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family of Ubume, Terumi and Juno rather than blood kin.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rights-card caste system and an employer whose trust must be regained.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Technocratic future of monitors and cards; no religion shown.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Paying 800 million yen for Juno's rights; survival dominates.

folkways.japan: The mujina (badger) name draws on Japanese folklore of shape-shifting tricksters, applied to an underclass living on Tokyo rooftops.

delivery.evidence: Outer Haven praises the gritty dystopia without calling it preachy; themes carried by the rights-card system and plot (VIZ blurb).

personified.ideology: rightless survival through skill and violence
streamer turned mujina, chaos for attention

delivery.note: The critique of rights for sale is built into the setting rather than argued in speeches, per the available review.

winners_losers: The rightless get the story's sympathy; the system that sells rights and those who exploit Juno are shown as the problem.
